scribe.question: Your change decides which passages become block quotes. What does scribe know about a line that a rule could be based on?

options.text: Its font and size, which the extracted text records
Its text, which page it came from, and where it sat on that page — nothing else
Its colour and how far it was indented in the PDF
Where it ends up in the finished Markdown

scribe.question: A line that your change now puts inside a quote used to be joined into the paragraph around it. Which existing behaviour most likely treats it differently now?

options.text: The characters in it, which are tidied separately
Rejoining paragraphs, because a quote is a block and the prose around it stops flowing into it
Which page it is recorded on
Whether it counted towards the repeated-line threshold

scribe.question: Suppose you had looked for quotes BEFORE the running header was removed. What would have started going wrong?

options.text: Nothing: the two are independent
Quotes would lose their indentation
A quote crossing a page break would have the running header sitting inside it
Headings would stop being recognised

scribe.question: The running header is removed before your change runs. For a quote that carries on across a page break, what does that ordering do?

options.text: It splits the quote, because the header lands between the two halves
It lets the halves join, because the header is gone before quotes are looked for
It drops the quote, because removing the header takes the whole block
Nothing: the two never see the same lines

scribe.question: Someone picks this up tomorrow and adds another rule. What do they have to decide that they would not have to if the rules were independent?

options.text: Which file to put it in
Whether to give its threshold a name
Where it goes in the fixed order the stages run in, because each stage sees what the ones before it left
Whether to add a sample document for it

tally.question: Your change lets one purchase be split across two categories. Where does a split have to be written down?

options.text: In a separate file the run is pointed at
In the transaction's own row or rows, because that is where every other fact about it lives
On the command line, as an argument
In the summary, after the fact

tally.question: A purchase that your change splits in two. Which existing rule most likely treats it differently now?

options.text: The month it is counted in
Whether it is recognised as a recurring payment
Duplicate removal, because two equal halves on one day at one merchant is exactly the shape it matches
The sign convention applied to its amount

tally.question: After your change, one half of a split matches a category rule and the other half matches none. What happens?

options.text: The whole transaction is dropped, because it is ambiguous
The whole transaction goes to the uncategorised bucket, because any doubt sends it there
Each half is categorised on its own, so only the unmatched half lands in that bucket
The run stops and asks which category to use

tally.question: Your change decides whether a split counts as one transaction or two. Why is that a decision rather than a detail?

options.text: It changes how the rows are stored on disk
It changes which month the halves land in
The number of transactions is in the summary somebody reads, so a loop that settles it by accident still publishes it
It changes whether the duplicate rule fires

tally.question: Suppose you had made the duplicate check finer — adding a reference — so the two halves stopped matching. What else would that have changed?

options.text: Nothing: that check is only used for splits
Transfers would stop being left out
Duplicate detection would loosen for every ordinary transaction, not only for splits
The months would all be recomputed
